questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point
questions.problem:
Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂z}=3{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)+3x{y}^{2}z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz)+3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)
$$

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(\pi ,-1,1):$

$$
\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂y∂y}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂z∂z}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂y∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂y∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)+3x{y}^{2}z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz)+3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)) \\  & =6y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)+6xyz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz)-3{x}^{3}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy).\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂z∂z} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂y∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(3{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)+3x{y}^{2}z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz)+3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)) \\  & =3x{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz)+3x{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz)-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)+6{x}^{2}z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(\pi ,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂y∂y}{|}_{(\pi ,-1,1)} & =6(-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+6(\pi )(-1)(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-3(\pi )^{3}(1)^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )=6\pi  \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂z∂z}{|}_{(\pi ,-1,1)} & =3(\pi )(-1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+3(\pi )(-1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-3(\pi )^{2}(-1)^{2}(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+6(\pi )^{2}(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )=-6\pi -6{\pi }^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂y∂y}{|}_{(\pi ,-1,1)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂z∂z}{|}_{(\pi ,-1,1)} & =6\pi +(-6\pi -6{\pi }^{2})=-6{\pi }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives
questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=4x+{y}^{2}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=4xy-y$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2x+y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=x+\sqrt{y}$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2xy+{y}^{2}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)={x}^{2}y+2x$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x+{y}^{2})=2y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy-y)=4y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+\sqrt{y})=1.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+{y}^{2})=2x+2y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y+2x)=2xy+2.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II only'.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives
questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

- ${f}_{x}(x,y)={e}^{-2x}-y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)={e}^{-y}-2x$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=5$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡xy+{y}^{2}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2xy\operatorname{cos}⁡xy+2xy$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{-2x}-y)=-1 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{-y}-2x)=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡xy+{y}^{2})=4y\operatorname{cos}⁡xy-2x{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2xy\operatorname{cos}⁡xy+2xy) \\  & =2y\operatorname{cos}⁡xy+2y\operatorname{cos}⁡xy-2x{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2y \\  & =4y\operatorname{cos}⁡xy-2x{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III only'.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives
questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2x-2{y}^{2}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=2y-2xy$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{x})$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)={e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡y$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=2{x}^{3}y-\sqrt{y}$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-2{y}^{2})=-4y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y-2xy)=-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{x}))=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2})=6{x}^{2}y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{3}y-\sqrt{y})=6{x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III only'.

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point
questions.problem: Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate ${f}_{yxy}(6,\frac{\pi }{3})$ if ${f}_{xy}(x,y)=7+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxy}(x,y) & ={f}_{xyy}(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{xy}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(7+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(6,\frac{\pi }{3}):$

$$
{f}_{yxy}(6,\frac{\pi }{3})=6\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})=3
$$
